results.title: Everyone’s Installing AI Agents. Nobody’s Building the System Around Them.
results.content:
Jeff Humble bought a €590 Mac Mini (about $600 USD), spent two days setting up OpenClaw, automated 1 out of 7 things he planned, and concluded: “The 🦞 didn’t replace Claude. It made me laugh instead.”

The pattern is always the same: install → basic setup → one cool demo → stop.

One person IS building a serious memory layer (the Behind the Craft podcast episode with Nat Eliason, where they talks about his OpenClaw build, is what gave me the idea that I could do it myself, but on a Raspberry Pi). But the broader community? Most people stop at install and cron jobs. The thing I find most frustrating about agents and AI is the lack of persistent memory. I wanted to see if I could build that capability and, if so, teach others how to do it.

## Why Raspberry Pi?

A few reasons: [...] Layer 3: Knowledge graph. Entity-based facts organized in a PARA structure. Each entity has structured items with source tracking, access counts, and decay classification (hot/warm/cold based on recency). These live in a directory structure on the Pi’s SD card under `life/`, all version-controlled in git.

Layer 4: Semantic search. OpenClaw’s built-in session memory indexes every conversation as embeddings. Nova can search across sessions in real time, so what was said in one Telegram topic is findable from another. Cross-session context without manual effort.

It sounds clean on paper. In practice, it broke. A few times. [...] Once I’d built out the memory architecture, I needed embeddings for semantic search. The Pi’s ARM processor wasn’t built for this kind of workload. Processing was too slow to be usable. Embedding generation for session transcripts kept failing at scale. Even with 8 GB of RAM, the chip just couldn’t handle the volume of text I needed to process.

This is the one area where a Mac Mini has a genuine advantage. Apple Silicon with unified memory can comfortably run 7B-13B parameter models locally through Ollama. But here’s the thing, most Mac Mini OpenClaw users aren’t actually running local models. They’re sending everything to the same API providers I am. The local inference advantage is real, but largely unused in practice.

results.title: Use Report a Concern to share feedback about Apple Intelligence - Apple Support
results.content:
If you have feedback about the response of an Apple Intelligence feature, you can share your response with Apple through Report a Concern, Apple’s built-in feedback mechanism. Apple will evaluate your feedback and may use what you’ve reported to help improve Apple products and services, for example to train models.

Apple Intelligence is currently in beta. It uses models, and the quality of outputs may vary. You should always check for appropriateness and accuracy.

## How to report a concern about an Apple Intelligence response

Report a Concern is the best way for you to provide feedback on output from Apple Intelligence features. Apple Support doesn’t have access to information about your prompt or the response, or the feedback that you provide through Report a Concern. [...] Look for the Report a Concern button on the screen.
 If you don't see Report a Concern, look for the More button or Options menu.
 Provide feedback about an Apple Intelligence response when you're viewing the response on your screen. If you’re not viewing the response, you can’t use Report a Concern.
 To provide feedback, you select from categories to help describe the issue. You also have the opportunity to provide additional information.
 When you submit feedback, Apple collects the information that you provide in your feedback report — including answers to questions, descriptions, photos, videos, messages, and emails. Before submitting, you can review and remove any information or attachments that you don’t want to include in your feedback report. [...] # Use Report a Concern to share feedback about Apple Intelligence

Your feedback is used to help improve Apple products and services, for example to train models.

## Share feedback to help improve Apple Intelligence

Apple Intelligence — the personal intelligence system built into iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Vision Pro — combines Apple-built models with your personal context to deliver intelligence that is most useful and relevant, all while protecting your privacy. Apple Intelligence is designed to understand and create language and images; prioritize and summarize notifications, mail, and messages; and draw on the personal information on your device to simplify and accelerate everyday tasks.

results.title: How do you prevent your AI agents from breaking in production?
results.content:
MCP tool access with no central governance. As your agents start calling external tools through MCP, every one of those connections needs its own o token. And right now, most teams are scrambling to manage this. There is no central place to see what agent has access to what. no audit trail from a security standpoint. That's not a gap. That's a liability. And your CISO will find it before your agents do. None of these things actually show up in staging. They are all problems that are never seen in a staging environment. They are all production problems and they all share a common root cause. There is nothing actually standing between your agents and the outside world that enforces control. This is where an AI gateway earns its place. Not as a routting convenience, but as the reliability [...] Second — latency spikes and traffic bursts. A provider slows down under load. Your enterprise rolls out an AI feature to 5,000 employees at 9 AM on a Monday. Without load balancing across deployments, your P95 latency blows up — and your agent feels broken even if it technically isn't.

Third — model quality degradation. This one is subtle and dangerous. Providers quietly update models. Response formats shift. A field your agent was parsing disappears. Your agent doesn't crash — it just starts returning wrong answers.

Fourth — cost blowouts. Agents are multi-step. One rogue loop, one misconfigured prompt, one edge case that triggers 50 LLM calls instead of 5 — and your monthly AI bill doubles overnight.
